figures.caption: Employing machine learning and genetic algorithms, we developed structurally enhanced antimicrobial peptides boasting exceptional efficacy.
figures.label: Figure 1

figures.caption: Identification of the substitution sites of amino acids that strongly affect the enhancement of anti-E. coli ability. a The first sequence logo represents the initial population of 9432 LBD sequences, which were generated through the process of roulette wheel selection drawing from fitness matrix (M3); The second sequence logo represents the final set of 313 optimized LBD sequences, which were generated by genetic algorithm with relative-MIC function; amino acids from the original and modified peptides are indicated by black and coloured letters, respectively. b Sequences of the synthesized peptides are presented, including the computational output LBDA-D, two randomly mutated LBDX and LBDY, and pGFP (as controls). The colour shading represents the substituted sites of amino acids.
figures.label: Fig. 3

figures.caption: Illustration of the machine learning-based algorithm used in this study. The first part of this algorithm is the construction and optimization module (COM), which accepts the input of the original peptide sequences used in this study and comprises three subprocesses, namely, fitness matrix construction, relative-MIC assignment and iterative exploration. The second part is strong substitution identification (SSI), which has been embedded in COM, and this is the module for the output of optimized peptide sequences.
figures.label: Fig. 1

figures.caption: Results from the physicochemical property investigation and fitness matrix construction processes. a Results of the initial fitness matrix M1 generated by PLSR and its derived final fitness matrix M3. b The Pearson correlation coefficient measurement indicates that the MICs and physicochemical properties are not simply linear. c and d FCM images indicating that LBD1-8 were the largest clusters created with hydrophobicity ranging from 0.5 to 0.7, a net charge of 2 to 7, and an isoelectric point of 10 to 12.
figures.label: Fig. 2

figures.caption: Antibacterial and morphological studies of LBDB. Killing indices showing that LBDB exhibited activity against E. coli (a and b), V. alginolyticus (g and h) and S. aureus (m and n) in a time-dependent (a, g and m) and dose-dependent (b, h and n) manner; SEM (c, d, I, g, o and p) showing that the cells of E. coli (d), V. alginolyticus (g) and S. aureus (p) were severely damaged after LBDB treatment due to cytoplasmic leakage in comparison with the controls (c, i and o); TEM showing that a series of pathological changes were observed on the cell surface of E. coli (f), V. alginolyticus (l) and S. aureus (r) with LBDB treatment compared with the control groups (e, k and q). The same capital letter represents no significant difference between the two groups, whereas the same letters in both uppercase and lowercase letters at one data point (time or concentration) represent significant differences between the two groups where uppercase and lowercase letters indicate p < 0.01 and p < 0.05, respectively.
figures.label: Fig. 4

figures.caption: Binding affinity test of LPS-LBDB. Compared with those of LPS-LBDMj and LPS, the UV intensity of LPS-LBDB was greater (250 nm) at the same concentration (a); the UV intensity of LPS-LBDB was directly proportional to the concentration of LBDB, substantiating the presence and strength of the molecular interaction.

figures.caption: 3D solution NMR structure of LBDB. Cartoon representation showing overlaid 20-lowest energy structures (left), a ribbon extended structure with two 310-helixes (middle, disulfide bond not shown), and electrostatic surface representation (right). NMR conditions: 700 MHz; LBDB was dissolved in water with 10 % D2O.
